title: Budget 2026: Modest short-term gains, big questions on living standards, devolution and tax choices
label: 3 November 2026 · Budget 2026 expert reactions
summary: Economists judged the Chancellor’s Budget as having almost no effect on medium-term growth, leaving a deep squeeze on household living standards, substantial uncertainty about public finances and major unanswered questions around devolution, defence spending and tax changes such as founders’ relief and temporary bank surcharges.

speakers.label: Professor Travers
speakers.name: Professor Tony Travers CBE
speakers.role: Interim Dean, LSE School of Public Policy

glossary.definition: Office for Budget Responsibility, the independent body that forecasts the UK's public finances and economy.
A measure of the government's underlying fiscal stance that removes the effects of the economic cycle and interest payments.
The Chancellor's contingency margin: extra space in the public finances before a fiscal rule is breached.
A limit set by the energy regulator on the typical household's annual energy bill.
Contracts for Difference: government contracts that guarantee a set price to renewable electricity generators.
Public financial institutions or public financial transactions used to fund projects off the usual departmental budget.
New city-regional or county-level governments proposed to receive devolved powers and some tax revenues.

chapters.title: Headline: minimal effect on growth
chapters.takeaway: Experts agree the Budget does almost nothing to change the UK's medium-term growth outlook.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Could each of you sum up how much difference last week's Budget will make to economic growth?

turns.speaker: Sanjay Raja
turns.text: The Budget was broadly as expected and very limited in growth effect. Our multipliers show almost zero impact overall—tiny bumps this year, then roughly zero, and small negatives later as the fiscal stance tightens.

turns.speaker: Helen Miller
turns.text: Looking through the 98 measures, there isn't anything to 'move the dial' on growth. Some small items might be sensible, but nothing large enough to change the medium-term rate.

turns.speaker: Professor Travers
turns.text: The fiscal devolution proposals start a long process that might boost growth eventually, but they won't affect the economy in the next year or two.

turns.speaker: Ruth Curtice
turns.text: I agree: the Budget won't lift the medium-term growth rate. If a simple measure could have done that, governments would've already taken it.

chapters.title: Living standards and the energy shock
chapters.takeaway: Household incomes are now forecast to rise far less in the 2020s, with energy prices and higher interest costs being key drivers.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The forecasts for household living standards are grim—are the new data points, like recent GDP, a reason for optimism?

turns.speaker: Helen Miller
turns.text: No. One quarter's GDP doesn't change the medium-term picture. The big uncertainty is inflation—driven by the war in the Middle East and energy prices—and that shapes living standards most.

turns.speaker: Ruth Curtice
turns.text: The projected hit to living standards is serious: the 2020s look far worse than the 2010s. The Government hasn't faced up to whom to protect in this squeeze; the recent one-off measures spread support too thinly.

turns.speaker: Bobby Dean
turns.text: If the Iran war eases and energy prices fall, would living standards recover significantly?

turns.speaker: Helen Miller
turns.text: Lower energy prices would help, but there is an underlying low-productivity problem too. Even if energy costs fall, boosting medium-term living standards requires many structural reforms across policy areas.

turns.speaker: Sanjay Raja
turns.text: There will be some scarring on savings and consumption. On energy specifics, the OBR's assumptions look optimistic versus market-based estimates—price-cap assumptions matter for next winter's squeeze.

chapters.title: Public finances, headroom and spending trade-offs
chapters.takeaway: Headroom has fallen; inflation and interest costs tighten real departmental spending and force difficult choices between public services and household incomes.

turns.speaker: Andrew Lewin
turns.text: Headroom fell from about £23bn to £15bn—did that drop happen or was it rebuilt by the Chancellor?

turns.speaker: Helen Miller
turns.text: The pre-measures forecast showed a bigger fall; the Chancellor topped it up slightly. But small swings matter: forecasts are uncertain and a modest shock can eat the buffer.

turns.speaker: John Glen
turns.text: Is the Iran war the main driver of the headroom movement?

turns.speaker: Helen Miller
turns.text: Yes—the war lifted inflation expectations and gilt yields, which raise interest costs and push borrowing up; that is the single biggest change between forecasts.

turns.speaker: Ruth Curtice
turns.text: Comparing headroom levels is tricky because the rules change. What matters is that borrowing is about £10bn higher on average—so the big picture is looser public finances and a harder trade-off in 2027.

turns.speaker: John Glen
turns.text: On defence: reaching 3% of GDP would squeeze other departments—how big is the funding gap?

turns.speaker: Helen Miller
turns.text: If you want health, welfare and defence to keep up in real terms, we estimate roughly a £28bn gap to fill. You can reallocate, cut, or raise tax—each choice has big consequences.

turns.speaker: Professor Travers
turns.text: A lot of the increased protected spending (NHS, benefits, defence) implies tighter funding for unprotected areas like local government—this is where devolution will begin life, in a constrained setting.

chapters.title: Devolution: big promise, many unanswered details
chapters.takeaway: Fiscal devolution could change growth patterns, but success depends on who gets what powers, capacity in new mayoral authorities, and how spillovers and equalisation are handled.

turns.speaker: Seema Malhotra
turns.text: Resolution Foundation flagged missed growth from closer EU ties; back to devolution—could decentralisation meaningfully raise growth?

turns.speaker: Ruth Curtice
turns.text: Devolution could help, but the Budget offered only the start of a long process. If the goal is more goods trade, that is a separate international issue; devolving powers helps local growth but isn't a silver bullet.

turns.speaker: Professor Travers
turns.text: ‘Rewiring the State’ implies big changes inside Whitehall and at the local level. MSAs will need huge capacity-building. Right now the policy lacks detail on roles, funding and how central departments will change.

turns.speaker: Helen Miller
turns.text: We need clarity on which spending responsibilities shift to mayors, what remains with councils, and whether deals will be bespoke or standardised—those choices determine the fiscal impact and growth potential.

turns.speaker: Ms Minns
turns.text: If devolving powers risks divergence between places, should the Chancellor accept that political risk to get higher growth in some regions?

turns.speaker: Sanjay Raja
turns.text: Devolution can help, but it must be accompanied by institutional capacity and equalisation choices—policy won't fit every place and uneven capability could widen regional gaps unless designed carefully.

turns.speaker: Professor Travers
turns.text: A paradox: despite large equalisation grants, regional inequalities persist. Devolution could incentivise competition or require more central tapering—Whitehall is likely to retain strong levers.

chapters.title: Tax policy choices: founders' relief, bank surcharge and compliance
chapters.takeaway: The Budget picked several controversial tax measures—founders' relief drew sharp criticism for being badly targeted, while a temporary bank surcharge and large compliance yields raise questions about permanence and realism.

turns.speaker: John Glen
turns.text: On tax strategy: did you spot any coherent, long-run tax reform in the Budget?

turns.speaker: Helen Miller
turns.text: No overarching strategy—many small changes. Founders' relief is especially poorly targeted: it hands big gains to successful founders and risks distorting behaviour rather than boosting productive entrepreneurship.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Can you spell out the flaws in founders' relief?

turns.speaker: Helen Miller
turns.text: It rewards people after they've 'made it', uses tight qualifying rules that founders can't predict, and creates perverse incentives—like selling too early—to capture a large tax break rather than support long-run scaling.

turns.speaker: John Glen
turns.text: Are there better models—like EIS/SEIS—that would encourage investment earlier?

turns.speaker: Helen Miller
turns.text: Yes. Schemes that give up-front relief when money is invested in firms are better targeted at growing businesses than a retroactive sale-time break.

turns.speaker: John Glen
turns.text: The Budget raised the bank surcharge temporarily to 6% for 15 months. Will that hit banks' competitiveness or be passed on?

turns.speaker: Sanjay Raja
turns.text: Because it is temporary and profit-based, the immediate competitive hit is limited, but evidence suggests such taxes can widen lending margins. Also, temporary measures often get reconsidered later—so permanence risk matters.

turns.speaker: Bobby Dean
turns.text: The Government expects big yields from cracking down on tax avoidance—are the planned HMRC gains credible?

turns.speaker: Helen Miller
turns.text: Ambitious. There is a genuine tax gap, so money is there, but yields from compliance are uncertain. The OBR has adjusted for uncertainty, but scoring risky revenue to pay for fixed spending is dangerous.

chapters.title: Energy policy, industrial support and practical fixes
chapters.takeaway: The Budget included steps to change how electricity levies are charged and to help energy‑intensive firms, but these are more about shifting who pays than making energy fundamentally cheaper; targeting household support matters.

turns.speaker: Chris Coghlan
turns.text: How much will the Contracts for Difference (CfD) moves reduce electricity prices?

turns.speaker: Sanjay Raja
turns.text: They help: our calculations give a modest reduction in wholesale electricity prices next year. CfDs and the broader cost-control framework help delink electricity from gas over time.

turns.speaker: Helen Miller
turns.text: CfDs move revenues around: they capture some generator profits and can lower levies on consumer bills, but someone still pays the subsidy. Auction prices will determine whether consumers win or lose overall.

turns.speaker: Ms Minns
turns.text: On household energy support, Resolution Foundation argued the policy was poorly targeted—what would you do instead?

turns.speaker: Ruth Curtice
turns.text: Rather than giving everyone the same small sum, target support by income and energy need. Poorer households and those with high gas needs should get larger help—practical admin limits exist, but targeting would be fairer and more effective.

turns.speaker: Chris Coghlan
turns.text: The Budget gave a 20–25% discount to some energy‑intensive firms—does that risk subsidising inefficient companies?

turns.speaker: Helen Miller
turns.text: It could. If it's industrial strategy aimed at internationally mobile firms, there is an argument for protection. If it's temporary crisis support, lowering unit prices weakens incentives to cut consumption. Targeting matters.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. If you have further written evidence, the Committee would welcome it—Helen, your founders' relief note, in particular.
